qs.q: A 50‑year‑old woman with a 3‑cm ovarian cyst is found to have a germline BRCA1 mutation; what prophylactic surgery is recommended to reduce her ovarian cancer risk?
qs.e: Risk‑reducing salpingo‑oophorectomy removes both ovaries and fallopian tubes, lowering ovarian cancer risk in BRCA1 carriers.

qs.q: A 35-year-old woman is found to have a large ovarian cyst filled with clear serous fluid and papillary projections. Psammoma bodies are noted histologically. What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Mature cystic teratoma of the ovary
qs.e: Psammoma bodies — concentrically laminated calcified concretions — are characteristic of serous tumours. They are found at the tips of papillary projections.

ai.title: Ovarian Cyst
ai.subject: Obstetrics & gynaecology
ai.summary: An ovarian cyst is a fluid‑filled sac arising from an ovary. Most are functional and resolve, but some require investigation for size, symptoms or complications, especially in low‑resource settings.

sections.p: A cyst is a fluid‑filled or partially fluid‑filled sac within or on the surface of an ovary, identified by pelvic examination or imaging.
b: Ultrasound (first‑line) shows anechoic, thin‑walled lesion for simple cysts
Complex features (septations, solid areas) raise suspicion for neoplasm

sections.p: Severity is graded by size, symptom burden and presence of complications.
b: Small (<5 cm), asymptomatic – watchful waiting
Medium (5–10 cm) or symptomatic – consider intervention
Large (>10 cm) or torsion/rupture – urgent management

sections.p: Cysts are classified as functional, pathological or iatrogenic.
b: Functional: follicular cyst, corpus luteum cyst – most common in reproductive age
Pathological: endometrioma, dermoid, cystadenoma, malignant tumor
Infection/ inflammation: tubo‑ovarian abscess in PID, especially with HIV or TB
Medication: clomiphene‑induced cysts

sections.p: Many are silent; symptomatic patients may have pelvic pain, pressure, menstrual irregularities or acute abdomen if torsion/rupture occurs.
b: Dull, unilateral lower‑abdominal pain
Sudden severe pain with nausea – think torsion
Irregular bleeding or amenorrhea

t.b: Is the cyst simple or complex? Simple → likely functional; complex → further work‑up
Is pregnancy present? Positive → consider ectopic or corpus luteum cyst
Is there a risk of ovarian malignancy? Elevated in post‑menopausal or complex cysts
Is there infection or inflammation? Raised WBC/ESR supports tubo‑ovarian abscess

t.a: If ultrasound unavailable – pelvic exam with bimanual palpation
t.b: Is a mass palpable? Gives size estimate, guides referral

sections.p: Complications can be life‑threatening and require urgent care.
b: Ovarian torsion – sudden severe pain, vomiting, peritoneal signs
Rupture – acute pain, hemoperitoneum, hypotension
Hemorrhage into cyst – drop in hemoglobin
Suspicion of malignancy – solid components, papillary projections, post‑menopausal age

sections.p: Management follows a stepwise approach: observation, medical therapy, or surgery.
b: Observe simple cysts <5 cm with repeat US in 6–12 weeks
Analgesia (paracetamol, NSAID if no contraindication) for pain
Hormonal contraception to suppress new functional cysts
If torsion suspected – urgent laparoscopy or laparotomy, attempt detorsion
Rupture with hemodynamic instability – fluid resuscitation, surgical exploration
Complex or >10 cm cysts – surgical removal (cystectomy or oophorectomy) after counseling

sections.p: Regular review prevents missed growth or malignancy.
b: Repeat US at 6‑12 weeks for cysts under observation
Educate on warning signs (sudden pain, vomiting, fever)
Consider combined oral contraceptives for recurrent functional cysts

sections.p: Conditions that mimic ovarian cysts on exam or imaging.
b: Uterine fibroid – solid, arises from uterus, may be pedunculated
Tubo‑ovarian abscess – complex mass with systemic infection signs
Ectopic pregnancy – positive β‑hCG, adnexal mass, amenorrhea
Simple cyst on US may hide early malignancy; correlate with age and CA‑125 if possible
Normal β‑hCG does not exclude early ectopic; consider clinical picture
Low CA‑125 in early ovarian cancer – do not rely solely on this marker

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden severe pelvic pain with vomiting
Signs of shock (low BP, rapid pulse)

faq.q: When is surgery indicated for an ovarian cyst?
faq.a: When the cyst is >10 cm, symptomatic, complex on imaging, torsed, ruptured with hemodynamic compromise, or suspicious for malignancy.

faq.q: Can a simple cyst become cancerous?
faq.a: Rarely; most simple cysts are benign, but persistent or enlarging cysts in post‑menopausal women need evaluation.

faq.q: What is the first step if torsion is suspected but ultrasound is not available?
faq.a: Proceed to urgent surgical exploration based on clinical assessment; delay for imaging can increase ovarian loss.

exam: A 22‑year‑old presents with unilateral lower‑abdominal pain and a 6‑cm cyst on US – what is your next step? — Assess for torsion (exam, vitals); if absent, observe with repeat US; if pain severe, consider analgesia and early surgical review.
How do you differentiate a functional cyst from an endometrioma on ultrasound? — Functional cysts are anechoic, thin‑walled; endometriomas are homogenous low‑level echoes ("chocolate cyst").

A patient with HIV has a complex adnexal mass and fever – what is the most likely diagnosis and initial management? — Tubo‑ovarian abscess; start broad‑spectrum IV antibiotics, obtain cultures, and arrange drainage or surgery.
Why is CA‑125 not reliable for screening in pre‑menopausal women? — It can be elevated in many benign conditions (endometriosis, PID) leading to false positives.
What are the contraindications to using NSAIDs for cyst‑related pain in this setting? — Active gastrointestinal ulcer, renal insufficiency, or concurrent anticoagulant therapy.
Explain why a large simple cyst (>10 cm) still often requires surgery even if asymptomatic. — Risk of torsion, rupture, and difficulty in monitoring; surgical removal reduces emergency complications.
In a low‑resource hospital without laparoscopy, how would you manage a suspected ovarian torsion? — Prompt laparotomy for detorsion or oophorectomy, after resuscitation and consent.
What counseling should be given to a woman with recurrent functional cysts? — Discuss hormonal contraception, lifestyle factors, and the importance of follow‑up imaging.
